text: Lesson 16 introduced Choice as one of the common field types, but it didn't say where the actual list of selectable values comes from — and the answer is a separate table entirely, called sys_choice, not the dictionary entry itself. The dictionary entry for a Choice-type field just says, in effect, this field's type is Choice. The specific values a user can pick from, New, In Progress, Resolved, and so on, are individual rows living in sys_choice, each one tied back to one specific table and one specific field.

A single sys_choice row carries, at minimum, the table and field name it belongs to, a label — the human-readable text shown in the dropdown, like In Progress — and a value, the underlying stored value, which is often different from the label. It also carries a sequence number controlling the order options appear in, and it can be marked inactive to retire an old option without deleting any historical record that still references it. System Definition, then Choice Lists, opens this table directly, filterable however you need.

Some Choice fields are dependent on another Choice field — the classic example being Category and Subcategory on Incident. Pick Hardware as the Category, and Subcategory narrows down to only the subcategories that make sense under Hardware: Laptop, Monitor, Printer, hiding everything that belongs to a different category entirely. Under the hood, each Subcategory row carries an extra value identifying its parent choice, and the form only shows rows whose parent matches whatever was picked above. This is configured on the dependent field's own dictionary entry, through its Dependent on field attribute.

A real example worth memorizing: Incident's priority field has five genuine out-of-box values — 1 Critical, 2 High, 3 Moderate, 4 Low, and 5 Planning. But here's the catch. In a correctly configured instance, priority usually isn't something an agent picks directly at all. It's calculated, derived from Impact and Urgency, each their own Choice fields, run through a priority lookup matrix built into the system. Set Impact to 1 High and Urgency to 1 High, and the platform computes Priority as 1 Critical without the agent ever touching that field.

Put the last three lessons together and you now have the whole picture: the dictionary entry sets a field's shape, sys_choice supplies its actual selectable values for Choice-type fields, dependent fields can cascade those values, and calculated logic like the priority matrix can override the field entirely. Next up: the dictionary lab, where you'll put all three of those pieces together yourself, by hand.
